query: Earlier refractory high-entropy alloys illustrate persistent trade-offs: MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW retained good yield strength from 600 to 1600 °C, with MoNbTaVW reaching 842 MPa at 1000 °C, but both had poor room-temperature fracture toughness and high density; HfNbTaTiZr showed room-temperature ductility above 50% and a yield strength of 929 MPa but only 295 MPa at 1000 °C; and as-cast HfMoTaTiZr achieved about 1600 MPa at room temperature and 855 MPa at elevated temperature but retained a density of 10.21 g cm−3. Given the constraint that density must be reduced without sacrificing the strong room- and high-temperature mechanical performance of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, what single intervention should be tested? Provide a mechanistic hypothesis, predicted outcomes relative to the as-cast baseline, explicit temperature and loading boundary conditions, supporting evidence from the preceding RHEA results, and a controlled experiment with quantitative rejection criteria that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Alloying as-cast HfMoTaTiZr with a small amount of Nb will reduce the density without sacrificing the strong room- and high-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.intervention: addition of a small amount of Nb
generation.conditions: room temperature and elevated temperature (up to 1000 °C)
generation.predicted_outcome: reduced density and maintained yield strength above 1600 MPa at room temperature and above 800 MPa at 1000 °C
generation.baseline: as-cast HfMoTaTiZr with a density of 10.21 g cm−3 and yield strength of 1600 MPa at room temperature and 855 MPa at elevated temperature
generation.boundary: temperature range from room temperature to 1000 °C and loading conditions of compression and tension
generation.uncertainty: the exact amount of Nb to be added and the resulting microstructure and properties

falsification_experiment.design: compression and tension tests at room temperature and elevated temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: if the yield strength at room temperature or elevated temperature is reduced by more than 10% or the density is not reduced, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. Several theoretical models of solid-solution strengthening have been proposed to explain how different constituent elements affect room-temperature or elevated-temperature strength [,]. We previously designed a RHEA that exhibited higher elevated-temperature strength and discussed the effect of the constituent elements on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys by using the subtraction method []. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add elements such as Mo, which significantly interact with the other elements. For higher elevated-temperature strength, one should add the elements that possess a high melting point such as Mo, Nb, or Ta. For higher ductility, one should add more Nb. With Ti or Zr addition, both the elevated-temperature strength and the density decrease.
